error_modes.label: Mission planning and route briefing conducted as a crew task

texts.0: SP, due to a threat that was present in the minimum threat set but not identified in the brief, planned the VFR navigation route as an individual task and briefed no division of duties between front and rear cockpit. SP covered neither the checkpoint sequence, nor the leg timing responsibility, nor the airspace and terrain constraints along the track. The IP had to stop the briefing and rebuild the route plan with SP before the sortie could be authorized.
texts.1: SP, due to mission planning that did not address the forecast weather at the recovery time, briefed the route without stating who would hold the chart, who would run the clock and who would fly. SP added the missing crew coordination content only after the IP had raised the point verbally more than once, and the plan was completed after the briefing had formally ended. No IP intervention was required in flight.
texts.2: SP, due to a first pass through the route flown without reference to the airspace boundaries along track, briefed the opening legs without assigning lookout and chart-reading responsibility. SP recognized the omission before the briefing ended, restated the division of duties for the whole route and flew the sortie as restated. No IP prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP planned the VFR navigation route as a crew task and briefed it accurately and without delay, with checkpoint sequence, timing responsibility, lookout duties and airspace constraints agreed before flight. SP identified the threats along the track in the brief and stated how each would be managed. The sortie was flown as briefed and no IP addition to the plan was required.
texts.4: SP planned every leg of the route as a crew task, including the contingencies for weather, unexpected traffic and checkpoint acquisition failure, and assigned duties for each of them. The brief was complete and unambiguous, the threats along track were identified and paired with a stated countermeasure, and deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard in planning and briefing the route as a crew task, but the crew coordination content was concentrated in the first legs and thinned out toward the turning point and the recovery. The trend across the brief was toward assuming the division of duties rather than stating it. SP is expected to brief duties, timing responsibility and threats for every leg of the route on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Use of the IFG/CRM matrix chart to highlight the applicable items

texts.0: SP, due to unfamiliarity with the publication, did not use the IFG/CRM matrix chart at any point of the navigation sortie and could not locate the items applicable to the profile. No matrix item was highlighted in the briefing and none was carried into the debriefing. The IP had to open the chart and work the applicable items with SP before the grade sheet could be completed.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete preparation during mission planning, opened the IFG/CRM matrix chart but highlighted items unrelated to the VFR navigation profile flown. SP selected the correct items only after repeated verbal direction from the IP, and their discussion was pushed to the end of the debriefing. No action beyond the extended debriefing was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed review of the chart before the brief, first highlighted a general matrix item instead of the one matching the navigation task actually flown. SP recognized the mismatch without prompting, returned to the IFG/CRM matrix chart and selected the correct items in time for the discussion. No IP direction was needed.
texts.3: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart accurately and without delay to highlight the CRM items applicable to the navigation sortie. The items selected matched the route flown and the areas covered in the debriefing, and were presented in the standard sequence.
texts.4: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart to highlight the applicable items and tied each one to a specific event of the route, from planning through the turning point to the recovery. The selection was complete, correct and required no revision by the IP, with negligible deviation from the expected standard.
texts.marginal: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart and met the standard, but selected the minimum number of items and needed a second look at the chart to confirm two of them. The trend was toward picking the familiar items rather than those matching the navigation profile actually flown. SP is expected to preselect the applicable matrix items during mission planning on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Crew communication and information sharing along the navigation legs

texts.0: SP, due to lack of communication of the recognized problem to the other cockpit, kept an unresolved position doubt to himself/herself and passed no checkpoint, timing or heading information for the whole leg. The IP had no means of knowing what SP believed the aircraft position to be until the track error had already taken the aircraft off the planned route. The IP had to take control of the navigation and reestablish the aircraft on track before the sortie could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to an indirect hint instead of a direct statement of the navigation state, passed checkpoint and timing calls that did not say whether the checkpoint had actually been identified. SP stated the position, the time and the heading correction clearly only after the IP had asked for them more than once, and the information arrived after the leg it referred to had been flown. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a high radio workload in the first part of the leg, omitted the checkpoint and timing call at the initial point and left the other cockpit without a shared picture of the navigation state. SP recognized the omission without prompting, passed a complete position, time and fuel update and maintained the agreed calls for the rest of the route. No IP prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP passed accurate and timely checkpoint, timing, heading and fuel information at each briefed point, so that both cockpits held the same picture of the navigation state throughout the route. Doubts about checkpoint identification were stated as doubts rather than left implicit, and radio and intercom transmissions did not compete with each other.
texts.4: SP kept the navigation state shared with the other cockpit continuously, stating the position, the confidence in it and the intended correction before being asked. Communication was structured, plain and separated from the radio calls in workload, and deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on sharing the navigation state, but the calls became shorter and less complete as the workload increased toward the turning point. The trend was toward passing the heading and omitting the fuel and timing elements of the update. SP is expected to keep the checkpoint, time and fuel content in every position call on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Workload distribution between aircraft control, navigation and lookout

texts.0: SP, due to poor workload distribution that left one crew member doing every job, attempted to fly the aircraft, read the chart, run the timing and transmit at the same time along the whole leg. Aircraft control and lookout were both abandoned while SP worked the chart head-down, and no task was passed to the other cockpit. The IP had to take control of the aircraft to restore the flight path and the lookout.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to shed a secondary task when workload increased, kept the chart work and the radio together during the turn onto the next leg and let the lookout lapse. SP passed the non-essential task to the other cockpit only after repeated verbal direction from the IP, and the rebalance came after the turn had been completed. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the chart work inside the turn, began the checkpoint search while still correcting the heading and briefly lost the outside scan. SP recognized the saturation without prompting, deferred the chart work until the aircraft was established on heading and reestablished the lookout. No IP prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP distributed the workload so that aircraft control, navigation and lookout were each served at the appropriate point of the leg, with chart work planned for the straight and level segments. Secondary tasks were deferred or passed to the other cockpit as workload rose, and the outside scan was maintained accurately and without interruption.
texts.4: SP anticipated the workload peaks of the route and moved the chart work, the fuel check and the radio calls clear of them before they occurred. Aircraft control and lookout were never displaced by a navigation task, and deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on workload distribution, but the rebalancing was reactive and came only once the outside scan had already narrowed. The trend was toward completing the chart task in progress rather than deferring it when the workload rose. SP is expected to plan chart and fuel work clear of turns and checkpoint acquisition on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Application of the CRM concept when analyzing route deviations and divert decisions

texts.0: SP, due to a briefed decision point that was passed without any decision being made, worked the deteriorating route situation alone and applied no CRM concept to the analysis. SP made no assessment of the remaining fuel, the weather ahead and the available alternates, and used neither the other cockpit nor the agencies available on the radio as a resource. The IP had to stop the navigation problem and direct the divert before the situation could be resolved.
texts.1: SP, due to the absence of explicit divert criteria in the mission brief, analyzed the unplanned route change on the basis of a single factor and did not state the alternatives to the other cockpit. SP considered fuel, weather and alternates together only after the IP had raised each of them verbally, and the decision was taken after the point at which it should have been made. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial focus on regaining the planned track, began the analysis of the weather ahead without stating the fuel available for the diversion. SP recognized the gap without prompting, restated the problem to the other cockpit with fuel, weather and alternates together and reached a decision within the leg. No IP direction was needed.
texts.3: SP applied the CRM concept to the maximum extent when analyzing the route deviation, stating the problem, the fuel and weather constraints and the available options to the other cockpit before deciding. The decision was made at the briefed decision point rather than after it, and the resulting plan was passed to both cockpits and to the controlling agency.
texts.4: SP treated the changed route situation as a crew problem from the first indication, defined the decision point and the criteria that would trigger the divert, and used every resource available inside and outside the cockpit. The analysis was complete, the decision was timely and reversible, and deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard in analyzing the route deviation as a crew task, but the options were stated only once the preferred plan had already been chosen. The trend was toward confirming the first solution rather than comparing the alternatives. SP is expected to state the divert criteria and the decision point before the leg on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Debriefing self-assessment and identification of CRM development areas

texts.0: SP, due to reviewing the sortie only by whether the checkpoints were reached, took no part in the CRM discussion at the debriefing and offered no assessment of the coordination errors made along the route. SP identified no area for CRM development and attributed the track and timing errors entirely to the conditions. The IP had to conduct the CRM debriefing alone and complete the CRM box of the grade sheet without any input from SP.
texts.1: SP, due to a debriefing prepared from memory without reference to the route log, described the navigation events but not the crew coordination behind them. SP identified a CRM development area only after the IP had named the events verbally more than once, and the discussion ran past the point where the remaining items could be covered. No further action beyond the extended debriefing was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial reconstruction of the sortie leg by leg rather than by crew action, first omitted the coordination failure at the turning point from the self-assessment. SP recognized the omission without prompting, raised the event, stated its effect on the route timing and proposed a specific improvement for the next sortie. No IP prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP assessed his/her own CRM performance accurately and without delay at the debriefing, identified the specific areas for development and stated where crew coordination had enhanced the navigation task and flight safety. The discussion covered the graded CRM items applicable to the sortie and the CRM box of the grade sheet was completed at the end of the debriefing.
texts.4: SP led the CRM portion of the debriefing, linked each coordination behavior to its effect on the route accuracy, the timing and the flight safety, and proposed measurable improvements for the next navigation sortie. The self-assessment matched the events as observed and required no correction by the IP, with negligible deviation from the expected standard.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard in the CRM self-assessment, but the areas identified were general rather than tied to the specific events of the route. The trend was toward accepting the IP's assessment rather than offering an independent one. SP is expected to bring two self-identified CRM development areas, referenced to specific points of the route, to the next debriefing.

error_modes.label: Exact transfer of A/C control phraseology and coordination of the shared navigation systems between cockpits
error_modes.source: technique:1.15 Transfer of A/C and Systems Control

texts.0: SP, due to using words such as it or jet in lieu of the term A/C, left the pilot flying role undefined at a checkpoint handover and released the controls before the other pilot had positively assumed them. SP did not shake the control stick and reconfigured the GPS and the RMU at the same moment, so both cockpits were making inputs on the A/C and on the same system under the last use, last in control logic. The IP had to state the transfer, take the controls and rebuild the route on the navigation display.
texts.1: SP, due to an abbreviated transfer call that omitted the term A/C, left the pilot flying role ambiguous while the other cockpit was resetting the RMU, and did not shake the control stick when assuming control. SP used the exact words only after the IP had directed it verbally more than once, and one EFIS change was made in the meantime without being communicated. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to attention on the next checkpoint at the moment of the handover, made the transfer call without noticeably shaking the control stick, leaving the assumption of control unconfirmed for a few seconds. SP recognized this without prompting, repeated I have the A/C with a positive shake of the stick, and stated which cockpit held the GPS before the next leg began. No IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP used the exact words You have the A/C and I have the A/C at every transfer and shook the control stick noticeably when assuming control, so only one pilot was flying at any point of the route. SP retained control of the canopy, RMU, GPS and EFIS unless a transfer of that system had been clearly communicated, and the other cockpit called the system back when finished. No IP prompting was required.
texts.4: SP applied the transfer phraseology as a fixed habit pattern in both directions, including the transfers directed by the IP during the navigation legs, and never relinquished control until the other pilot had positively assumed it. Systems use was coordinated item by item, so no inadvertent input occurred on the navigation displays, and the intercom failure alternative was briefed and rehearsed. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on transfer of A/C and systems control, but the confirming stick shake was weak on two handovers and the term A/C was replaced once by an informal word. The trend was toward relying on the other cockpit to infer both the transfer and the ownership of the GPS rather than stating them. SP is expected to use the exact phraseology with a positive stick shake, and to call the system transfer, on every handover of the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Checklist discipline in the cruise legs - challenge and response on (BOTH) items and recovery after interruption

texts.0: SP, due to giving lip service to the checklist by reciting the standardized mnemonic instead of actually performing the required check, omitted items on more than one checklist during the route. SP treated the (BOTH) items as complete without receiving a proper response from the pilot not flying, and started a new checklist before the previous one had been completed. The IP had to stop the navigation task and run the checklists from the top with SP.
texts.1: SP, due to accepting an interruption at a checkpoint without a restart point, resumed the checklist at the step believed to be next rather than restarting at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step. SP left one (BOTH) item unconfirmed until the IP had prompted it verbally more than once, and completion of the checklist was never positively confirmed. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a radio call arriving in the middle of the checklist, lost the place for a few seconds and initially resumed at the wrong step. SP recognized this without prompting, restarted two to three steps prior to the interrupted step and re-challenged the (BOTH) item until a proper response was received. No IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP positively confirmed completion of every checklist during the route, challenging each (BOTH) item and treating it as complete only after a proper response from the other cockpit. SP attempted each checklist without interruption, did not start a new one before finishing the previous one, and kept the checklist out of the critical phases of flight. No IP prompting was required.
texts.4: SP executed a few items from memory and then referenced the checklist page to verify completion, so no item was carried on assumption at any point of the navigation profile. Every (BOTH) item produced an explicit challenge and response, and the two interruptions of the sortie were absorbed by restarting at the first step without any effect on the leg timing. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on checklist discipline, but the confirmation of completion was implicit on two checklists and one (BOTH) item was logged after only a nod from the other cockpit. The trend was toward using the mnemonic as a substitute for the check itself once the workload of the leg increased. SP is expected to positively confirm completion and to obtain a spoken response on every (BOTH) item on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Verbal compensation for the tandem cockpit - independently set altimeters and cockpit specific systems

texts.0: SP, due to failing to compensate with verbal communication for the lack of inter-cockpit visibility, assumed the A/C configuration for the next leg without verifying it with the other cockpit. The altimeter settings, which are set independently in each cockpit, were never cross checked, so the two cockpits were flying the terrain clearance of the route against different references. The IP had to intervene, restate the setting and correct the altitude flown over the leg.
texts.1: SP, due to judging the intentions of the other cockpit from control feel rather than from a spoken statement, did not confirm the altimeter setting at the new area pressure and could not state which items were controlled only from the front cockpit. SP made the cross check only after the IP had requested it verbally more than once, and the discrepancy stood for the greater part of the leg. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to concentrating on the checkpoint identification, delayed the altimeter cross check with the other cockpit after the area change. SP recognized the omission within a few seconds of the next checkpoint, called the setting, confirmed it back from the other cockpit and stated who held the systems that can only be manipulated in the front cockpit. No IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP compensated for the limited visibility of the other cockpit with explicit verbal communication, confirming A/C systems configuration and intentions at each leg change. Altimeter settings were called and confirmed in both cockpits, and SP knew which systems can only be operated or directly checked from the front or the rear cockpit. No IP prompting was required.
texts.4: SP made the state of the A/C explicit before it could be misread, verifying bleed air, OBOGS and defog operation by the described indirect checks and confirming the altimeter setting at every pressure change. Intentions for the coming leg were stated in advance so the other cockpit could anticipate the actions rather than deduce them. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on tandem cockpit coordination, but the verbal confirmation of configuration followed the action instead of preceding it, and the altimeter cross check was prompted once by the other cockpit. The trend was toward assuming that the other cockpit could see and infer what was being done. SP is expected to state configuration changes and to initiate the altimeter cross check at every setting change on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Operations checks at the prescribed interval with continuous update of the closest divert field

texts.0: SP, due to allowing the checkpoint and landmark identification task to consume the whole of the crosscheck, performed no operations check over the route and never updated the closest divert field. Fuel state, engine indications and the divert option were unknown to the crew when the profile was already well into the second half, and the radio frequencies were not managed for the next sector. The IP had to direct the operations check and establish the divert plan for the crew.
texts.1: SP, due to deferring the operations check until a workload gap appeared, exceeded the 15 to 20 minute interval by a wide margin and carried a divert field that had been left behind two legs earlier. SP performed the check and updated the divert field only after the IP had prompted it verbally more than once. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a course and airspeed correction at the previous checkpoint, let the operations check slip past the 15 to 20 minute interval. SP noticed the slip without prompting at the next checkpoint, completed the check, updated the closest divert field and reported the fuel state to the other cockpit. No IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP performed operations checks every 15 to 20 minutes throughout the route and updated the closest divert field at each of them, reporting the result to the other cockpit. Radio frequencies for the coming sector were managed in advance, and the timing between checkpoints was maintained alongside the checks. No IP prompting was required.
texts.4: SP tied the operations check to the checkpoint sequence so it always fell inside the prescribed interval without competing with the navigation task, and stated the closest divert field with its heading, distance and fuel required. Frequency management was anticipated one sector ahead, so no check was displaced by a radio task. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on the operations check cadence, but two checks fell at the far end of the 15 to 20 minute interval and the divert field was stated without the associated fuel figure. The trend was toward performing the check as a report rather than as a decision input. SP is expected to run the check at the mid point of the interval and to state heading, distance and fuel to the closest divert field on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Operational risk management of the route - environmental conditions, mission profile and pilot factors

texts.0: SP, due to not identifying the risks of the planned profile at an acceptable level, assessed neither the environmental conditions, nor the mission profile, nor the pilot factors before flying the route. The low level segment and the uncontrolled airfield were accepted as planned with a marginal weather and bird status, and no mission change was considered. The IP had to reject the plan and restructure the profile before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to treating the risk assessment as a paperwork step rather than a trade of training benefit against risk, covered the weather but omitted the bird status, the index of thermal stress and the pilot factors of experience, fatigue and currency. SP produced the missing elements only after the IP had asked for them more than once, and the mitigation offered was to cancel the segment rather than to modify it. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to the attention given to the route calculations, initially assessed only the environmental conditions and omitted the mission profile factors. SP recognized the gap during the same briefing without prompting, added the formation, VFR, low level and uncontrolled airfield considerations and proposed a mission change that did not reduce the training value. No IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP identified the risks of the sortie across environmental conditions, mission profile and pilot factors, and reduced them to an acceptable level with changes that did not negatively impact the training objectives. The goal of matching risk to the mission, rather than eliminating it, was stated and applied in the choices made for the route. No IP prompting was required.
texts.4: SP carried the risk assessment into the air, revisiting it when the observed weather, the turbulence or the fatigue level differed from the values assumed in planning, and adjusted the profile accordingly. Each mitigation was chosen so that the training benefit of the leg was preserved, and the reasoning was shared with the other cockpit. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on operational risk management, but the pilot factors were addressed generically and no in flight revision of the assessment was made when the conditions changed over the route. The trend was toward completing the assessment once, on the ground, and then holding the plan unchanged. SP is expected to reassess the environmental, profile and pilot factors at the mid point of the route on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Airborne flying safety - clearing the airspace and an emergency recovery plan established before the emergency

texts.0: SP, due to allowing a converging A/C and a systems indication to cause distraction during a critical phase of the route, stopped clearing the airspace and stopped monitoring the A/C systems altogether. No emergency recovery plan had been established before the situation developed, so the crew had neither a field nor a heading available when it was needed. The IP had to take the controls, clear the flight path and nominate the recovery field.
texts.1: SP, due to fixing attention on the unexpected traffic instead of maintaining the perception of self and A/C in the dynamic environment, let the systems monitoring and the lookout lapse over the leg. SP restated the recovery plan only after the IP had directed it verbally more than once, and the plan was limited to the departure field regardless of the position along the route. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to the appearance of a converging A/C during a checkpoint turn, momentarily narrowed the scan to that A/C alone. SP recovered the full clearing pattern within a few seconds without prompting, resumed the systems crosscheck and confirmed with the other cockpit the recovery field valid for the current leg. No IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP cleared the airspace and monitored A/C systems continuously through the route, and kept an emergency recovery plan established ahead of any malfunction rather than built after one. Distractions from traffic and from cockpit indications were absorbed without loss of the perception of position, altitude and mission state. No IP prompting was required.
texts.4: SP forecast the tasks of each leg from the current picture and moved the emergency recovery plan forward with the A/C, so the nearest suitable field was known at every point of the route. Traffic and systems events were handled as anticipated inputs rather than as surprises, with no interruption of the navigation crosscheck. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on airborne flying safety, but the recovery plan was updated only at the turning points and twice lagged the actual position of the A/C. The trend was toward rebuilding situational awareness after a distraction rather than protecting it while the distraction was present. SP is expected to state the current recovery field at each operations check and to hold the clearing pattern through traffic events on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Dedicated crew briefing block for inter-cockpit responsibilities and business-like conduct of the debriefing

texts.0: SP, due to spending excessive time on S.O.P material that should already be committed to memory, left no part of the briefing for the crew discussion of inter-cockpit responsibilities, emergency procedures and crew coordination. The minimum of 5 minutes for the crew briefing was not allowed at all, and in the debriefing SP took the critique of execution personally and did not accept the instruction offered. The IP had to interrupt, brief the crew responsibilities and reset the tone of the debriefing.
texts.1: SP, due to reading the standard items line by line instead of briefing them as standard, compressed the crew discussion well below the 5 minute minimum and covered the emergency procedures only nominally. SP opened the inter-cockpit responsibilities only after the IP had directed it more than once, and the debriefing had to be redirected from justification to the issues affecting the sortie. No further IP action on the plan was required.
texts.2: SP, due to the time taken by the route and weather portions, initially skipped the crew coordination block of the briefing. SP recognized the omission before the step and added the inter-cockpit responsibilities, the emergency procedures and the transfer of control agreements within the remaining time. The debriefing was then conducted in a business-like manner with the critique received openly.
texts.3: SP allowed at least 5 minutes for the crew briefing and used it for inter-cockpit responsibilities, emergency procedures and crew coordination, briefing as standard the elements covered by the S.O.P. The majority of the briefing time was spent on the how to of the navigation profile, and the debriefing covered the areas needing improvement without personalizing the critique. No IP prompting was required.
texts.4: SP delegated the supporting briefing tasks appropriately, protected the crew coordination block from compression and set clear objectives and standards by which the sortie would be measured. In the debriefing SP reconstructed only the amount of the mission needed to address the issues, used the instruction openly as a tool for improvement and carried the points forward into the next plan. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on the crew briefing and debriefing, but the crew coordination block was held to the bare minimum and the emergency procedures were briefed as a list rather than as agreed actions. The trend was toward protecting the S.O.P portion of the briefing at the expense of the crew portion. SP is expected to allocate the full crew briefing block first and to brief standard elements as standard on the next sortie.
